title: Old Testament Foundations of the Trinity

keyTerms.d: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4) — the heartbeat of Israel's faith, confessed against a world crowded with gods. Any honest discussion of the Trinity and the Old Testament has to begin here, on Israel's own ground, and refuse to leave it. On Richard Bauckham's reading, Second Temple monotheism was "strict," defined not by bare numerical oneness but by the unique identity of the one God: the only Creator, the only sovereign, the only rightful recipient of worship.

Scripture's own category (Hebrews 1:1–2): God's self-disclosure unfolds over time, seed to flower — the suffering Messiah, the bodily resurrection, the inclusion of the Gentiles are each foreshadowed in the older books and revealed fully only later. On this view the Old Testament gives shadows, not statues — but shadows are cast by something. The claim is not that Moses taught Nicaea.

keyTerms.t: The Angel of the LORD (mal'akh YHWH)
keyTerms.d: The figure who appears to Hagar, to Abraham, to Moses at the burning bush, and to Jacob — who speaks as the LORD, is identified as the LORD, and bears the Name ("my name is in him," Exodus 23:21), yet is somehow distinct from the LORD who sends him. Identity and distinction held together in a single character.

Passages that set the LORD beside the LORD: Genesis 19:24, "the LORD rained... fire from the LORD out of heaven" — the LORD on earth and the LORD in heaven side by side; Psalm 110:1, "The LORD says to my Lord"; and Zechariah 2, where on one natural reading YHWH says YHWH has sent him, though the sender/sent referent here is debated. None of these, alone, demands two persons; together they form a pattern the Old Testament never resolves and never disowns.

God's Word by which the heavens were made (Psalm 33:6), the Wisdom beside him as a master craftsman at creation (Proverbs 8), and the Spirit who can be "grieved" and rebelled against (Isaiah 63:10) and is named alongside God as sending a speaker (Isaiah 48:16) — not three persons yet, but the canon repeatedly drawing distinctions within the one God.

keyTerms.t: Two powers in heaven (shtei reshuyot ba-shamayim)
keyTerms.d: The early rabbinic category of heresy Alan Segal documented — readings that found a second divine figure beside the LORD. The decisive point is methodological: you do not legislate against an interpretation no one holds, so the controversy is evidence that the texts themselves generated binitarian readings inside Judaism, many of them apparently before and apart from the church.

The strongest explanation of Genesis 1:26's "Let us make" — God addressing his heavenly court, the "sons of God" and angelic council attested across the Old Testament — favored by many critical scholars and held by the trinitarian Michael Heiser, who warns against using the verse as a Trinity proof-text. The next verse's singular "God created" shows that only God does the creating. This reading is granted; the case does not rest on the verse.

The "one like a son of man" who comes "with the clouds of heaven" — elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible God's own conveyance — and receives an everlasting dominion, a second figure in the one heavenly scene that the vision never explains. Who the figure is remains genuinely debated: an exalted angelic representative (Collins: most likely Michael), or a heavenly individual (Boyarin, a contested minority). The clouds are the stronger half of the case; the service-verb (pelach) can denote either religious worship or the service owed to a king.

derive.q: Christians confess one God in three coequal persons, a doctrine fixed at Nicaea and Constantinople centuries after the Hebrew Scriptures were complete. So does the Old Testament TEACH that doctrine?
derive.ans: no — and we should say so plainly
derive.why: Ancient Israel was monotheistic, and no Israelite prophet ever set out a doctrine of three persons in one essence. The narrower, more defensible question is whether the Old Testament, within its fierce monotheism, leaves a kind of unexplained plurality that the New Testament later names.

derive.q: For centuries some Christians treated "Let us make man" (Genesis 1:26) as if it simply proved the Trinity. Should the case rest on it?
derive.ans: no — leave the verse out entirely
derive.why: The plural has natural explanations in its ancient setting, and the divine-council reading may well be the plain sense — Michael Heiser holds it and warns against using the verse as a proof-text. Anyone who claims Genesis 1:26 "proves" three persons has overreached, and should stop. So the verse carries no weight here and we do not ask it to.

derive.q: Take the threads singly — the Angel, the Word, Daniel's son of man — and each has an innocent explanation. So why does the pattern still press?
derive.ans: because the same shape keeps emerging from independent devices
derive.why: Different vocabularies, different genres, different centuries all keep generating one silhouette: something that is of God, with God, and acting as God, distinguishable from the LORD who sends it yet never a second god. When a tradition's ordinary literary machinery repeatedly throws off the same figure, the figure has become data, not decoration.

derive.q: Israel's own guardians had to mount a sustained polemic against "two powers in heaven." What does the very existence of that controversy show?
derive.ans: the puzzle is native to Judaism, not a Christian import
derive.why: You do not legislate against an interpretation no one holds. The controversy is evidence that the texts themselves generated binitarian readings inside Judaism — many apparently before and apart from the church. It shows the texts were genuinely suggestive, not that the suggestion was thereby proven true.

derive.q: Grant every thread and every Jewish witness. Does the Old Testament, on its own, get you to Nicaea's three coequal persons?
derive.ans: no — the foundations are not the house
derive.why: The Old Testament foundation does not, on its own, get anyone to Nicaea; the leap from "unexplained plurality" to "three coequal persons" is supplied by the fuller revelation. What it does is more limited and more important: it shows the triune God is the kind of God Israel's Scriptures were already describing — so the confession completes Israel's story rather than betraying it. The doctrine is established on other grounds: revelation and the resurrection.

honestState.p1: Genesis 1:26's "Let us make" is best left out of the case entirely — the divine-council reading may well be its plain sense, and even the trinitarian Michael Heiser warns against using it as a proof-text. The weight falls elsewhere: the Angel who is both identified as YHWH and distinct from him; the two-YHWH texts (Genesis 19:24); the Word, Wisdom and Spirit acting as God with God; and Daniel 7's figure coming with the clouds. Honest limits: Psalm 110:1's second "Lord" is adoni, a title used of human masters too; Daniel's pelach can denote either worship or the service owed to a king, and who the figure is remains debated; none of these, alone, demands two persons. The core warrant is convergence — the same silhouette emerging from independent devices — not any single verse.
honestState.fairness: The Jewish alternatives are not desperate and must be met at full strength. John J. Collins reads Daniel's figure as an exalted angelic representative, most likely Michael; Hebraists defend the "plural of deliberation"; Michael Heiser holds the divine-council reading of Genesis 1:26. Daniel Boyarin's bolder claim — that a "binitarian" Judaism was widespread and that the divine-human redeemer is itself a Jewish idea rooted in Daniel 7 — is contested, and Peter Schäfer and others judge it an overreading, though even his critics grant that the conceptual room existed. Richard Bauckham and Larry Hurtado reframed the field around a "strict" monotheism of unique identity and an early "binitarian/dyadic" devotion to Jesus; how elastic Jewish monotheism was is a genuine live dispute. Jewish scholars who document "two powers" readings emphatically do not endorse them as true.
honestState.verdict: The foundations are not the house. The Old Testament does not teach the doctrine of the Trinity — ancient Israel was monotheistic, the developed dogma is later, and the plurals and the Angel can each be read otherwise; anyone who claims Genesis 1:26 "proves" three persons has overreached and should stop. But it does present the one God as internally rich and self-differentiated in ways Israel never explained away, and it left those tensions live enough that Israel's own interpreters had to argue about "two powers" long before any Christian creed. So the objection that the Old Testament rules out the Trinity does not hold: it does not contradict the Trinity; it answers questions the Old Testament itself raised. The doctrine is established on other grounds — revelation and the historical case for who Jesus was — and this is what we hold to be true: the one God exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three coequal, coeternal persons, one God.

order: The Hebrew Bible repeatedly presents plurality within the one YHWH — the Angel, the two-YHWH texts, the Word, Wisdom and Spirit, and Daniel 7's figure coming with the clouds (Genesis 1:26's "Let us make" is deliberately NOT on the list).
Early Jewish interpretation wrestled with the same texts, many readings apparently before and apart from the church — the puzzle is native, not imported.

Therefore the Old Testament does not rule out the Trinity; it answers questions the Old Testament itself raised — it does not teach the doctrine or prove it, and the positive case rests on revelation and the resurrection.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: P1: the Hebrew Bible repeatedly presents plurality within the one YHWH — the Angel who speaks as YHWH and bears the Name (Ex 23:21) yet is sent by YHWH, the two-YHWH texts (Gen 19:24), the Word, Wisdom and Spirit acting as God with God, and Daniel 7's heavenly figure coming with the clouds. Precision: Genesis 1:26's "Let us make" is deliberately NOT on the list, and the OT does not teach the doctrine — it gives shadows, not statues.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: P2: these are not Christian retro-readings — early Jewish interpretation wrestled with the same texts (the "two powers in heaven" controversies, Daniel 7's thrones, the Targums' creating Memra), many of them apparently before and apart from the church. Precision: that a community read a second power out of the texts shows they were suggestive, not that the suggestion was correct.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the Trinity does not collide with the Old Testament — it answers questions the Old Testament itself raised, and the triune God is the kind of God Israel's Scriptures already describe. It does NOT teach or prove the doctrine, and it does not get anyone to Nicaea on its own; the positive case rests on revelation and the resurrection.

cards.q: Why is Genesis 1:26's "Let us make" deliberately left OUT of the case — even though Michael Heiser is a trinitarian?
cards.a: Because the plural has natural explanations in its own setting — a plural of deliberation, a plural of majesty, or God addressing his heavenly court — and that council reading may well be the plain sense (Heiser holds it and warns against proof-texting the verse). Anyone who says it "proves" three persons has overreached and should stop. The verse carries no weight here; the case rests on convergence elsewhere.

cards.q: What is the convergence argument, and why does it turn a suggestion into data?
cards.a: Take each thread singly and each has an innocent explanation; the question is why the same shape keeps emerging from independent devices — the Angel, the Word, the Wisdom, the Name, the Glory, the Spirit, the second figure of Daniel 7 — all generating one silhouette: of God, with God, acting as God, distinguishable from the LORD who sends it yet never a second god. When a tradition's own machinery keeps throwing off the same figure — and its guardians must police "two powers" to suppress it — the figure has become data, not decoration.

cards.q: What makes the Angel of the LORD more than an ordinary envoy?
cards.a: The envoy (shaliach) convention explains speech — an emissary spoke in the sender's full authority. But conventional envoys do not bear the divine Name within them, and of this figure God says, uniquely, "my name is in him" (Ex 23:21); nor do they prompt a man to say he has seen God's face and lived (Gen 32:30). Identity and distinction are held together in one character.

cards.q: Why do the rabbinic "two powers in heaven" debates matter to this case?
cards.a: You do not legislate against an interpretation no one holds. That the rabbis had to combat "two powers" readings is evidence the texts themselves generated the puzzle inside Judaism — many readings apparently before and apart from the church. It shows the texts were genuinely suggestive, not that the suggestion was thereby proven true.

cards.q: What does Daniel 7 contribute — and what is its honest limit?
cards.a: A heavenly "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds — elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible God's own conveyance — and receives an everlasting dominion, a second figure in the one heavenly scene that the vision never explains. Honest limit: who the figure is remains genuinely debated (Collins reads an exalted angel, most likely Michael; Boyarin, a contested minority, a heavenly individual), and the service-verb pelach can mean either worship or the service owed to a king. The clouds are the stronger half; treat the service-verb as suggestive, not decisive.

cards.q: Reply to: "The LORD is one" — the Shema rules out any plurality.
cards.a: Granted that the Old Testament is fiercely monotheistic, and any reading that turns the Shema into a confession of three gods has misread it catastrophically. But Isaiah's "alone" and "by myself" exclude every rival and every creature — the heavenly council included — from the work of creation; they do not legislate on the inner life of the one Creator. So the objection that the Old Testament rules out the Trinity does not hold.

cards.q: Reply to the hardest objection: "generated binitarian readings" is not the same as "true."
cards.a: Accurate as a description of what the Old Testament can do on its own, and we concede it — it does not get anyone to Nicaea. What it does is more limited and more important: it shows the triune God is the kind of God Israel's Scriptures were already describing, so the confession completes Israel's story rather than betraying it. The doctrine is established on other grounds: revelation and the resurrection.

cards.q: How should the claim be calibrated — and what pattern does it follow?
cards.a: Seed, not statue — the Old Testament raises the questions the Trinity answers; it does not state the doctrine. Shadows, not statues, but shadows are cast by something. It is the ordinary shape of progressive revelation: the suffering Messiah, the resurrection, and the Gentile mission are each seeded, wrestled over within Israel, and unveiled fully only later.

cards.q: Does the Old Testament case, by itself, establish the doctrine of the Trinity?
cards.a: No — the foundations are not the house. They do not secure the coequality and coeternity the creeds insist on, and they certainly do not teach three gods (tritheism), one person in three masks (modalism), or a lesser second god (subordinationism). But foundations are not nothing: they tell you the house belongs on this ground and no other. And this is what we hold to be true — the one God exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three coequal, coeternal persons, one God.

obj.q: Doesn't "Let us make man in our image" (Genesis 1:26) just prove the Trinity — God talking among the persons?
obj.model: Largely granted — and this is exactly where popular apologetics overreaches. The divine-council interpretation is a serious, perhaps the most defensible, reading of that single verse; Michael Heiser, who has done as much as anyone to revive the divine-council framework, takes "let us" as God's address to his heavenly host and warns against using it as a Trinity proof-text. Anyone who claims Genesis 1:26 "proves" three persons has overreached, and should stop. So the verse carries no weight here and we do not ask it to. But the council reading does not erase the pattern; it relocates the question. Granting that "let us make" addresses the heavenly host still leaves Genesis 1:27's singular "God created" insisting the image-bearing creation is God's act alone, and still leaves Daniel 7's heavenly figure coming with the clouds — elsewhere God's own conveyance — to receive an everlasting dominion, a scene the council reading of Genesis does nothing to explain.

obj.q: The Angel of the LORD is just an envoy — a shaliach speaks in the full authority of the one who sent him, so of course he speaks as the LORD. And Wisdom in Proverbs 8 is personified poetry, like Folly a few verses later.
obj.model: The envoy convention really does explain a great deal of the Angel's speech, and Wisdom in Proverbs 8 really is, in its first sense, personification — grant both. But the envoy convention explains speech, and conventional envoys do not bear the divine Name within them; of this figure God says, uniquely, "my name is in him" (Exodus 23:21), and they do not prompt a man to say he has seen God's face and lived. Personified Wisdom is poetry, but personified Folly is never placed beside God at creation. If the case rested on any one of these threads it would fail — but it rests on none of them singly; it rests on the convergence of all of them.

obj.q: The Old Testament doesn't merely fail to teach the Trinity — it relentlessly teaches the opposite. "The LORD is one." "I am the first and the last; besides me there is no god." Isaiah says the LORD made the heavens "alone," "by myself." A plurality smuggled into that polemic isn't a discovery; it's a contradiction.
obj.model: The Old Testament is monotheistic, and any reading that turns the Shema into a confession of three gods has misread it catastrophically — that should simply be granted. But Isaiah's "alone" and "by myself" exclude every rival and every creature — the heavenly council included — from the work of creation; they do not legislate on the inner life of the one Creator. The Christian claim was never three gods; it is one God, internally rich and self-differentiated, within that fierce monotheism. So the objection that the Old Testament rules out the Trinity does not hold: the Trinity does not contradict the Old Testament; it answers questions the Old Testament itself raised. The positive case rests on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was.

obj.q: All you've shown is that the Old Testament is suggestive and that some ancient Jews found it so — which is a long way from true. The leap from "unexplained plurality" to "three coequal persons" is supplied entirely by the New Testament, not the Old.
obj.model: As a description of what the Old Testament can do on its own, that is accurate, and we concede it. The Old Testament foundation does not, on its own, get anyone to Nicaea. What it does is more limited and more important: it shows that the Trinitarian God is the kind of God Israel's Scriptures were already describing — so the Christian confession is the completion of Israel's story rather than a betrayal of it. The doctrine is established on other grounds — revelation and the resurrection; the Old Testament shows it has deep and native roots.

unseen.q: Fine — grant that the Old Testament hints at a second divine figure. But the earliest Christians who read it that way, like Justin Martyr, made that figure a lesser, subordinate "second God" under the Maker of all. So your Old Testament "foundations" don't lead to your coequal Trinity at all — they lead to a demoted second god. You've proved subordinationism, not the Trinity.
unseen.model: That is honest, and it marks a real limit — the early Christian use of these texts was sometimes theologically rougher than later orthodoxy. When Justin Martyr argued from the Angel and from Genesis 18–19 that there is "another God and Lord" beside the Maker of all, he did frame that second figure as in some sense subordinate — language the church later judged inadequate and corrected at Nicaea, which confessed the Son as "true God from true God... of one being (homoousios) with the Father." So the concession stands: the Old Testament foundations point toward plurality-in-unity, but they do not, by themselves, secure the coequality and coeternity that the creeds rightly insist on, and they certainly do not teach three gods (tritheism), or one person in three masks (modalism), or a lesser second god (subordinationism). Those refinements come from the fuller New Testament revelation read as a whole. But notice what the convergence actually keeps throwing off: a figure "distinguishable from the LORD who sends it yet never a second god" — of God, with God, acting as God, within Israel's fierce monotheism. That is precisely the shape a coequal Trinity completes, not the shape of a demoted deity bolted beside the first. The doctrine is established on other grounds — revelation and the resurrection; the Old Testament shows only that it has deep and native roots.
